about.p: Every unit is two pages. The **left-hand page** teaches about 20 to 30 words and phrases on one everyday topic, in sections A, B and C, with examples, *Common mistakes* and tips. The **right-hand page** practises them: matching, gap-fills, sorting words into groups and finding the odd one out. *Over to you* asks you to write about your own life with the new words.
The units are grouped by topic (People, At home, Leisure…). You can study them in any order, but it helps to do a block of units on the same topic.

about.-: **Today** gives you new words from the next unit every day, then checks them straight away. Words come back for review after 1, 3, 7, 16, 35, 90 and 180 days. The book says you need to meet a word five to seven times before you really know it: the reviews do that for you.
**Units**: read the left-hand page (tap a word to hear it and to open its card), then press *Start practising*. Score 80% or more to pass the unit.
**Over to you**: write about yourself with the new words. Your writing is saved, so you can come back to it.

about.tip: Keep a vocabulary notebook, as the book suggests: on each word card you can write your own sentence, and it is saved in *My writing*.

L.p: Most family words come in pairs: one for a man or boy, one for a woman or girl. Your *relatives* (or *relations*) are all the people in your family.

L.e: Have you got any brothers and sisters? – No, I'm an only child.
Do you come from a big family? – Yes, I've got three brothers and two sisters.

L.x: We say *my wife* (one) but *their wives* (more than one).

L.!: British people often ask *Have you got…?* about family: Have you got any cousins? Have you got any children?

L.p: Some words for clothes are always plural and take a plural verb: *My trousers are new.* To count them, say *a pair of*: two pairs of jeans, a pair of glasses.
You *wear* clothes, but you *carry* things like a bag or an umbrella. You can also say *She's got a blue coat on.*

L.e: In the morning you get dressed. At night you get undressed.

L.x: You *put* clothes *on* and you *take* clothes *off* (not *put clothes off*).

L.tip: When you get dressed, say to yourself: Now I'm putting on my socks. Now I'm putting on my shoes…

L.!: In British English a *jumper* or *sweater* is a warm top. *Trainers* are sports shoes (American English: sneakers).
